learning.javascript:
A singly linked list is a linear data structure made up of nodes, where each node stores a value (.value) and a pointer (.next) to the following node. The last node's .next pointer is null, marking the end of the list.

Reading the picture: the list is known by its head, its first node. Each node holds a value (here, a word) and next, which leads to the following node. To reach "World!", start at the head and follow next once. The last node's next is null: there's nothing after it.

It's called singly linked because each node knows only the node after it. (A doubly linked list also gives each node a link back to the one before.)

In JavaScript, .next holds a reference to another node object: setting a.next = b doesn't copy b, it makes a point at it.

Making and linking nodes

Back to front, passing each node the one after it:

const c = new SinglyLinkedListNode("C");
const b = new SinglyLinkedListNode("B", c);
const a = new SinglyLinkedListNode("A", b);   // a is the head

Or front to back, setting .next as you go:

const head = new SinglyLinkedListNode("A");
head.next = new SinglyLinkedListNode("B");
head.next.next = new SinglyLinkedListNode("C");

Either way the result is A -> B -> C -> null, and the function returns the head.

Nodes you no longer reach are cleaned up automatically by JavaScript's garbage collector.

Walking the list

To visit every node, start at the head and keep following next until you reach null. Printing as you go is a good way to check a list you've built: when you press Run, anything your code prints appears in the console's stdout tab.

let node = head;
let out = "";
while (node !== null) {
    out += node.value + " -> ";
    node = node.next;
}
console.log(out + "null");   // A -> B -> C -> null

The same walk is how you'd add to the end of a list of any length: keep going until you reach the node whose next is null, and set that node's next to the new node.

Why use a linked list?

Compared with an array:

  • Adding at the front is cheap. Make a node whose next is the old head, and it becomes the new head. An array would have to shift every element along.
  • Reaching the k-th item is slow. An array jumps straight to it; a linked list has to walk k steps from the head.

learning.cpp:
A singly linked list is a linear data structure made up of nodes, where each node stores a value (.value) and a pointer (.next) to the following node. The last node's .next pointer is nullptr, marking the end of the list.

Reading the picture: the list is known by its head, its first node. Each node holds a value (here, a word) and next, which leads to the following node. To reach "World!", start at the head and follow next once. The last node's next is nullptr: there's nothing after it.

It's called singly linked because each node knows only the node after it. (A doubly linked list also gives each node a link back to the one before.)

In C++, next really is a pointer: its type is SinglyLinkedListNode*, the memory address of the following node. When you have a pointer to a node, reach its fields with -> rather than .: head->value, head->next. (a->b is shorthand for (*a).b.)

Making and linking nodes

Back to front, passing each node the one after it:

SinglyLinkedListNode* c = new SinglyLinkedListNode("C");
SinglyLinkedListNode* b = new SinglyLinkedListNode("B", c);
SinglyLinkedListNode* a = new SinglyLinkedListNode("A", b);   // a is the head

Or front to back, setting next as you go:

SinglyLinkedListNode* head = new SinglyLinkedListNode("A");
head->next = new SinglyLinkedListNode("B");
head->next->next = new SinglyLinkedListNode("C");

Either way the result is A -> B -> C -> nullptr, and the function returns the head.

Make nodes with new, not as local variables. A local such as SinglyLinkedListNode a("A"); is destroyed when the function returns, so returning &a would leave the caller a dangling pointer to memory that's gone. new creates the node on the heap, where it stays until it's deleted (new expression, storage duration). Real programs delete nodes when they're finished with them, or use smart pointers. Here the judge reads your list after your function returns, so leave them.

Walking the list

To visit every node, start at the head and keep following next until you reach nullptr. Printing as you go is a good way to check a list you've built: when you press Run, anything your code prints appears in the console's stdout tab.

for (SinglyLinkedListNode* node = head; node != nullptr; node = node->next) {
    cout << node->value << " -> ";
}
cout << "nullptr" << endl;    // A -> B -> C -> nullptr

The same walk is how you'd add to the end of a list of any length: keep going until you reach the node whose next is nullptr, and set that node's next to the new node.

Why use a linked list?

Compared with an array:

  • Adding at the front is cheap. Make a node whose next is the old head, and it becomes the new head. An array would have to shift every element along.
  • Reaching the k-th item is slow. An array jumps straight to it; a linked list has to walk k steps from the head.

description.javascript:
A singly linked list is a linear data structure made up of nodes, where each node stores a value (.value) and a pointer (.next) to the following node. The last node's .next pointer is null, marking the end of the list.

You are given the SinglyLinkedListNode class below, which takes a .value and an optional .next pointer. Using only this class, construct a singly linked list where each node holds one word from the phrase "Hello World!", in order, and return the head of the list.
